Studs Terkel, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author, broadcaster, actor and activist whose interviews preserved the experiences of working people and others often absent from traditional histories, died at his Chicago home at the age of 96.

Over a career spanning more than half a century, Terkel became one of America’s most recognizable oral historians. Armed with a tape recorder, a quick wit and an extraordinary ability to listen, he invited people to describe their lives in their own words. Factory workers, nurses, farmers, teachers, executives, veterans, immigrants and civil rights activists all found a place in his books and radio programs.

Terkel won the 1985 Pulitzer Prize for general nonfiction for *“The Good War”: An Oral History of World War II*. Rather than presenting the conflict solely through military leaders and official accounts, the book gathered the recollections of soldiers and civilians, including those whose memories complicated the popular image of World War II as an unambiguously noble struggle. The quotation marks in its title reflected Terkel’s skepticism toward simple or romantic versions of history.

His other major works included *Division Street: America*, a portrait of urban life and social divisions; *Hard Times*, an oral history of the Great Depression; and *Working*, a landmark collection of interviews about how Americans viewed their jobs and what they sought from them beyond a paycheck. Later books examined race, aging, hope and the search for meaning.

Born Louis Terkel in New York City in 1912, he moved with his family to Chicago as a child. The city became his lifelong home and the center of his work. After earning undergraduate and law degrees from the University of Chicago, he pursued acting and broadcasting rather than practicing law.

Terkel first gained broad attention in radio and television. His Chicago television program, *Studs’ Place*, presented an informal world of conversation and music, but his outspoken political views hurt his career during the anti-communist climate of the 1950s. He later built a lasting home at Chicago radio station WFMT, where his long-running interview program featured authors, musicians, politicians, performers and ordinary citizens. His guests ranged from celebrated cultural figures to people rarely heard on the air.

Though he interviewed the famous, Terkel’s deepest interest was in everyday experience. He approached oral history not simply as documentation but as a democratic act. His books allowed people to speak with their own rhythms, contradictions, humor and anger. He edited their testimony into vivid collective portraits without erasing the individuality of the speakers.

Terkel was also a committed progressive who supported labor unions, civil rights, free expression and peace movements. He remained publicly engaged well into old age, criticizing war and inequality while encouraging younger generations to challenge injustice. His activism, like his writing, was rooted in the conviction that history belonged not only to presidents and generals but also to the people who worked, struggled and endured outside the spotlight.

With his rumpled appearance, red socks and ever-present tape recorder, Terkel became a beloved Chicago figure. More importantly, he helped redefine whose stories were worth preserving. **CHICAGO —** Studs Terkel, the radio interviewer and Pulitzer Prize-winning oral historian who transformed the experiences of workers, soldiers and ordinary citizens into an enduring record of 20th-century America, died October 31, 2008, at his Chicago home. He was 96.

His son, Dan Terkel, said his father died quickly and without pain after years of declining health. “He had a very full, very satisfying and long life,” he told The Associated Press.

For more than half a century, Terkel listened to people whom history often overlooks: factory hands and farm laborers, nurses and teachers, civil-rights activists, veterans, immigrants, the unemployed and the wealthy. With a tape recorder, an unmistakable rasp and an instinct for conversation, he made their memories the substance of history.

The quotation marks around “good war” signaled his skepticism about simple accounts of heroism and victory. In a past CNN interview, he summed up one of the convictions running through his work: “War is always about betrayal” — particularly the betrayal of the young by the old and of soldiers by political leaders.

Among his other influential books were *Division Street: America*, *Hard Times: An Oral History of the Great Depression*, *Working*, *The Great Divide*, *Race* and *Coming of Age*. *Working*, published in 1974, examined what Americans did all day and how they felt about it. The book later inspired a Broadway musical.

Born Louis Terkel in New York City on May 16, 1912, he moved with his family to Chicago as a child. His parents operated a rooming house, where he encountered the parade of characters and conversations that helped shape his lifelong curiosity. He earned undergraduate and law degrees from the University of Chicago but chose performance and broadcasting over a legal career.

He became known as “Studs,” a nickname linked to James T. Farrell’s *Studs Lonigan* novels. After working in theater and government radio projects, he became a Chicago television personality and, later, one of the country’s most distinctive radio interviewers. His program on WFMT ran for decades and featured guests ranging from musicians and writers to politicians and labor organizers.

Colleagues remembered that Terkel’s gift lay less in interrogation than in attention. He approached interviews as conversations, allowing pauses, digressions and contradictions to remain. His longtime collaborators said he was intensely prepared but never rigid, and that his enthusiasm could make celebrated artists and anonymous workers feel equally important.

That democratic spirit also defined his politics. A committed New Deal liberal and outspoken defender of unions and civil liberties, Terkel was blacklisted during the McCarthy era after refusing to disavow progressive causes. He remained an opponent of racial injustice and later criticized the Iraq War and government surveillance.

In interviews with CNN, Terkel repeatedly argued that Americans needed to recover both memory and conversation. “We’re suffering from national Alzheimer’s disease,” he said, warning that a society unable to remember its past was vulnerable to repeating it. He also stressed the simple principle behind his life’s work: people should talk — and, just as importantly, listen — across differences.

His wife, Ida Goldberg Terkel, whom he married in 1939, died in 1999. Their marriage lasted six decades.

Terkel continued writing and speaking well into his 90s, despite heart surgery and a fall at his home. Age diminished neither his curiosity nor his indignation. He remained recognizable by his red-checked shirt, rumpled manner and ever-present cigar, though it was the sound of his voice — gravelly, amused and urgently interested — that most listeners remembered.

For Terkel, history was not chiefly the story of presidents and generals. It was the accumulated testimony of people describing what they had endured, believed, built and lost. His achievement was to ask the questions, keep the recorder running and let them be heard.

Terkel, who was not conventionally religious, approached the subject with curiosity rather than doctrine. He was interested in how people endured the knowledge of death, what they believed might follow it, and how remembrance could resist disappearance.

His later years included the death of his wife, Ida, in 1999 after six decades of marriage. He underwent open-heart surgery in his 90s but continued giving interviews and working on books. Even as his hearing and mobility declined, he remained publicly engaged, speaking against war and warning that Americans too easily forgot the struggles behind labor rights and civil liberties.

That concern with memory ran through his final works. **“Hope Dies Last”** examined people who maintained political and social commitments despite defeat. His last collection, **“P.S.: Further Thoughts from a Lifetime of Listening,”** returned to the themes that had defined him: curiosity, resistance, historical memory and the worth of individual testimony.

Terkel’s politics were openly left-wing, rooted in the labor movement, the New Deal and the civil rights struggle. Admirers saw him as a humane populist; critics sometimes found him sentimental or ideologically predictable. But even those who disagreed with him recognized the scale of the record he assembled.

His legacy lies partly in the thousands of voices he preserved. Before podcasts and digital storytelling made first-person testimony commonplace, Terkel demonstrated that extended conversation could be documentary art. He helped popularize oral history for a mass audience and influenced journalists, historians, broadcasters and writers.

More broadly, he insisted that history was incomplete without the testimony of people who rarely appeared in official accounts. His America was noisy, divided and unfinished. It lived in lunchrooms, factories, union halls, kitchens, hospital rooms and front porches — wherever people tried to explain what had happened to them.

Terkel approached death as he had approached work and history: by asking questions and listening for answers that did not fit neatly together. He left no final theory of American life. Instead, he left a chorus — contentious, wounded, comic and resilient — in which ordinary people could hear themselves as participants in history rather than as its background.
